ABSTRACT

This

dissertation

departs

from

the

the

maxim

as

the

—

analyst

and

analysand

Drawing

Cassin's

Jacques

the

which

psychoanalysis

to

this

rehabilitation.

We

argue

that

this

contribution

can

be

located

primarily

in

two

moments

of

Lacan's

work.

The

first

concerns

Lacan's

critique

of

the

analyst's

position

in

relation

to

knowledge,

particularly

in

Seminars

11

and

12.

By

refusing

the

crystallization

of

the

subject

supposed

to

know

and

theorizing

what

the

analyst's

desire

would

be,

Lacan

teaches

that

the

analyst

operates

not

as

one

who

has

an

answer

for

everything,

but

as

a

semblance

of

object

a

—

this

being

the

alternative

solution

Lacan

proposes

to

the

problem

of

non-being

as

presented

in

Plato's

Sophist
.

The

second

moment

concerns

the

language

with

which

psychoanalysis

works:

a

logos

that

is

not

an

organon

—

an

instrument

for

the

communication

of

being

—

but

a

pharmakon
,

whose

efficacy

is

performative,

that

is,

it

produces

effects

of

discourse.

To

think

through

this

efficacy,

the

research

locates

in

L'Étourdit

(1972-1973)

a

new

proposal

concerning

the

analyst's

saying

—

insofar

as

it

is

effective

—

consisting

in

the

formula

of

interpretation

as

a

particular

apophantic

that

cuts

through

the

modal

envelope

of

the

sayings

and

reveals

the

cause

of

desire.

Without

dismissing

all

that

has

already

been

said

about

the

analyst's

listening,

we

privilege

the

approximations

between

the

function

of

speech

in

sophistics

and

in

psychoanalysis

as

derived

from

our

reading

of

L'Étourdit
.

From

this

perspective,

psychoanalysis

approaches

sophistics

not

only

by

working

with

the

equivocity

of

language,

but

also

by

assuming

that

saying

produces

effects

upon

the

world

—

and

it

is

precisely

in

this

that

the

possibility

of

both

pathos

and

cure

resides.
